chapter_title: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
learning_objective: The learner will assess whether their own probability judgments, and those of two weather forecasters, are overconfident, underconfident, or well calibrated, by stating probabilities for twelve statements and judging the results against a reliability table, with all three assessments correct.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** calibration-confidence-game
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/confidence-calibration-challenge
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** assess
**Learning Objective:** The learner will assess whether their own probability judgments, and those of two weather forecasters, are overconfident, underconfident, or well calibrated, by stating probabilities for twelve statements and judging the results against a reliability table, with all three assessments correct. **Prerequisites:** probability, prediction uncertainty, model calibration, overconfident, underconfident, Brier score (defined in "Prediction Uncertainty" and "Model Calibration" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** Three committed judgments, each with one attempt: (1) after stating probabilities for the twelve statements and seeing their reliability table, the learner judges their own record as overconfident, about right, or underconfident; it is correct when it matches the verdict computed by Rules; (2) the learner judges which of Forecaster A and Forecaster B is better calibrated; (3) the learner judges whether Forecaster B was overconfident or underconfident. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Stating the twelve probabilities is the data for judgment 1, not itself evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Being confident is the same as being well calibrated (Forecaster B; statements answered at 100 percent). (2) A 70 percent forecast is "wrong" whenever the event does not happen (Forecaster A). (3) Saying 50 percent on everything is a safe strategy (the 0.25 baseline). (4) Twelve answers are enough to know one's calibration for sure (the small-sample note). **Instructional Rationale:** Evaluate-level work asks the learner to judge a record against a standard. Generating their own record first makes the judgment personal and exposes overconfidence directly, and the two forecasters give a second, cleaner case in which the standard can be applied without the learner's own stakes. **Content:** Part A: twelve statements, shown one at a time in this order. The learner states the probability that each statement is true. | # | Statement | True or false | Why (shown after the learner commits) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Mount Parnassus rises more than 2,000 m above sea level. | True | It rises to 2,457 m (Chapter 17). | | 2 | Delphi is more than 300 km by road from Athens. | False | It is about 180 km, about two and a half hours by coach (Chapter 18). | | 3 | The Oracle of Delphi gave answers for more than 1,000 years. | True | From at least about 750 BCE to 391 CE, about 1,140 years (Chapter 17). | | 4 | The Byzantine Empire lasted longer than the oracle did. | False | The Byzantine Empire lasted 1,123 years; the oracle about 1,140 (Chapter 17). | | 5 | Herodotus wrote down the Croesus prophecy within 20 years of the fall of Sardis. | False | He wrote about 115 to 120 years later (Chapter 17). | | 6 | Joseph Fontenrose collected more than 500 Delphic responses. | True | He collected about 535 (Chapter 17). | | 7 | More than 4,000 lead question tablets survive from the oracle of Zeus at Dodona. | True | More than 4,000 survive (Chapter 17). | | 8 | The Temple of Apollo whose ruins we saw at Delphi was finished in the 6th century BCE. | False | It was finished around 330 BCE, in the 4th century; the 6th-century temple burned in 548 BCE (Chapter 17). | | 9 | At Salamis, Athens supplied almost half of the Greek ships. | True | 180 of 378 ships, about 48 percent (Chapter 15). | | 10 | The council of the Amphictyonic League had 24 votes. | True | Twelve member peoples with two votes each (Chapter 17). | | 11 | Fewer than 100 records of freed slaves survive at Delphi. | False | More than a thousand manumission records survive (Chapter 18). | | 12 | The Athenian Treasury at Delphi was rebuilt from its original blocks in the 20th century. | True | French archaeologists rebuilt it between 1903 and 1906 (Chapter 18). | Totals: 7 true (1, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12) and 5 false (2, 4, 5, 8, 11). Part B: two forecasters' records (illustrative), shown after Part A. | Forecaster | Forecast | Days | Days with rain | Brier score | |---|---|---|---|---| | A | 70% chance of rain | 10 | 7 | 0.21 | | B | 90% chance of rain | 10 | 6 | 0.33 | Judgment questions: | # | Question | Choices | Correct | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | J1 | Looking at your reliability table, how calibrated were you? | Overconfident; about right; underconfident | The verdict computed by Rules | Your average confidence was [c]% and you were right [h]% of the time. | | J2 | Which forecaster is better calibrated? | A; B | A | A said 70% and it rained on 7 of 10 days; B said 90% and it rained on 6 of 10. | | J3 | Was Forecaster B overconfident or underconfident? | Overconfident; underconfident | Overconfident | B's 90% came true only 60% of the time, so B claimed more certainty than the record supports. | Notes always shown with the results: "Twelve answers is a small sample; forecasters are judged over hundreds." and "Saying 50% on everything scores 0.25: never wrong, never useful." **Provenance:** Statements 1 to 12 and their reasons come from Chapters 15, 17 and 18 of this book, as cited in each row; the sim copies them verbatim. Forecaster records are illustrative and labeled "Illustrative records." The Brier score values are computed from the Rules and match the chapter's worked example in "Model Calibration." **Rules:** - Probability input for each statement: minimum 0, maximum 100, step 10, default 50, unit percent; it means "the chance this statement is true." - The learner must commit a probability before the answer and reason are shown; a committed probability cannot be changed. - Brier score: the mean over all twelve statements of (p − o)², where p is the probability as a fraction (0.0 to 1.0) and o is 1 if the statement is true and 0 if false. Range 0.00 to 1.00, shown to two decimals; lower is better. Baseline for always answering 50 percent: 0.25. - Leaning: p > 50 means the learner leans "true" with confidence p; p < 50 means the learner leans "false" with confidence 100 − p; p = 50 means no lean. A leaned statement is a hit when the lean matches the truth. - Reliability table: one row for each confidence level 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 percent, showing the number of leaned statements at that level, the number of hits, and the percentage of hits; a row with no statements shows "none." - Verdict for J1: compute c = mean confidence of leaned statements and h = percentage of leaned statements that were hits. Overconfident if c − h > 10 percentage points; underconfident if c − h < −10; about right if −10 <= c − h <= 10. - J1 unlocks only if at least 6 of the 12 statements are leaned (p ≠ 50). If fewer are leaned, the sim says "Lean one way on at least 6 statements so there is a record to judge," and offers Try Again. - The verdict, c and h are shown only after J1 is committed; the reliability table and Brier score are shown before. - Try Again clears all twelve probabilities, the judgments and the scores. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads statement 1 and sets a probability that it is true. 2. The learner presses Commit; the truth and the reason appear. 3. The learner continues through all twelve statements. 4. The sim shows the learner's Brier score, the 0.25 baseline, and the reliability table. 5. The learner answers J1, judging their own calibration from the table; the verdict with c and h appears. 6. The learner sees the two forecasters' records and answers J2 and J3. 7. The learner should notice whether their 90 and 100 percent answers were right as often as they claimed, and that Forecaster B's confident record scored worse than the 50 percent baseline. **Feedback:** For each statement after Commit: "True." or "False." followed by the reason, and "Your score on this one: [(p − o)² to two decimals]." For J1, J2 and J3: correct shows "Correct:" plus the Why text; incorrect shows "Not quite:" plus the Why text. One attempt each; the correct answer is shown after the attempt. At the end: if J1, J2 and J3 are all correct, "You can judge a forecaster, including yourself: confidence has to be earned by the record."; otherwise, "Compare the stated percentage with the percentage that came true, row by row." **Starting State:** Statement 1 is shown with the probability set to 50 percent, a Commit control, and the question "How likely is this to be true?" **Chapter Anchors:** Forecaster A: 70 percent on ten days, rain on 7, Brier score 0.21. Forecaster B: 90 percent on ten days, rain on 6, Brier score 0.33, overconfident by 30 points. Always saying 50 percent scores 0.25. Twelve statements from this book.
